analysis.one_liner: Lets communities and gun-violence victims sue firearm makers, dealers, and importers in federal court.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new federal lawsuit right against gun manufacturers, dealers, and importers. Any state, city, organization, business, or person hurt by gun violence — or stuck paying its bills — could sue a gun company that knew or should have known its design, marketing, sales, or distribution practices would likely lead to gun violence. Courts could award actual and punitive damages, plus attorneys' fees and expert witness costs. The bill never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, whose taxpayers currently pay the medical, policing, and cleanup costs of gun violence, plus individual victims, community organizations, and businesses hurt by shootings. Trial lawyers handling such suits would also gain a new fee-shifting claim.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting states, local governments, organizations, businesses, or individuals injured by — or bearing costs from — gun violence sue manufacturers, dealers, or importers whose practices would likely result in gun violence, overriding conflicting state and federal law.

Allows courts to award actual damages, punitive damages, attorneys' fees, expert witness costs, and other appropriate relief, so plaintiffs who could not afford to sue get their litigation costs covered.
Applies to both intentional unlawful use and unintentional discharges of firearms, and lets plaintiffs sue in federal or state court.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers, dealers, and importers, who would face costly litigation, damages awards, and pressure to change how they design, market, and distribute guns. Higher liability costs could also translate into higher prices for gun buyers.

drawbacks.text: The liability standard — 'knew or reasonably should have known' that practices would likely result in gun violence — reaches beyond traditional products liability and could expose lawful dealers to expensive lawsuits over third-party crimes, raising litigation costs across the industry.

A 'should have known' standard gives courts broad discretion and could produce unpredictable, inconsistent judgments against the industry, which the bill's own findings acknowledge as a rationale for a uniform federal rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts real, documented costs of gun violence — medical care, policing, lost life — onto the companies whose sales and distribution practices fed it, with fee-shifting that makes suits affordable for cities and victims. The cost is genuine legal exposure for an entire lawful industry, including dealers whose only connection is selling a legal product that was later misused, and the loose 'should have known' standard makes outcomes hard to predict. A more carefully drawn liability standard could have targeted the same harm with less collateral risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey, joined by Rep. Carolyn McCarthy, introduced the bill on March 23, 1999, to let governments and gun-violence victims sue firearms manufacturers, dealers, and importers in federal or state court.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The bill had 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican — and remained stuck in committee until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and importers, who avoided a new federal liability regime and the litigation costs that would have come with it; state and local budgets continue to absorb the costs of gun violence.

for.name: Rep. Nita M. Lowey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal cause of action against gun manufacturers, dealers, and importers for gun-violence harms.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Joined Lowey in introducing the bill on the day of introduction.

for.name: 11 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 23, 1999 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; support was heavily Democratic (10 of 11 cosponsors were Democrats), but the only record is sponsorship, not how the chamber would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed the entire firearms trade to federal lawsuits for gun-violence costs, with punitive damages and fee-shifting designed to make such suits routine. The industry's interest was in keeping those costs off its books, while governments and victims keep paying them.
The bill pays attorneys' fees and expert witness costs, making gun-violence suits financially viable for governments, victims, and the lawyers who represent them.
